findings.fix_hint: move mkstemp inside the try (initialise tmp_path=None and skip the unlink when it is None), or wrap it in its own OSError handler that logs and returns
findings.problem: `fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")` runs before the `try:`. The docstring (D-17) says file-write failure is non-fatal and that OSError is never re-raised. mkstemp can raise OSError in several cases: the config directory is read-only (for example a read-only Docker volume mount), it is out of space or inodes, or it has the wrong ownership. That error leaves `_write_reset_token_file`, passes through `run_in_executor`, and propagates out of `reset_request_post` at routes.py:1698 with no handler. By then the token is already minted into app.state and written to the log, so the user gets a 500 instead of the neutral confirmation, and the failure skips the sanitized error log the function promises. A config dir that is not writable is the scenario this non-fatal path was designed for.
findings.title: tempfile.mkstemp sits outside the try, so a config-dir OSError becomes an unhandled 500
findings.why_it_matters: The recovery endpoint returns a server error in exactly the read-only or full-disk deployments where the file sink fails, which contradicts the documented D-17 guarantee.

findings.fix_hint: track whether fdopen took ownership and os.close(fd) in the except/finally when it did not
findings.problem: mkstemp returns a raw OS fd. Only the `with os.fdopen(fd, ...)` block closes it. If `os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)` raises OSError (for example EPERM on some network or FUSE filesystems), or if os.fdopen itself fails, the except branch logs the error and unlinks tmp_path but never calls os.close(fd). The `finally` closes only dir_fd. The whole acquire-to-release scope is in this function.
findings.title: Raw fd leaks if os.fchmod (or os.fdopen) raises before the file object owns it
findings.why_it_matters: Each failed reset request leaks a file descriptor in a long-running daemon.

I also traced the downstream path in triggarr/logging.py: `setup_logging()`'s `buffer_sink` redacts using that same `secrets` list and then stores the unredacted token text in the in-memory `log_buffer` (triggarr/log_buffer.py, maxlen=200). That buffer is read by the existing `/` dashboard route and the `/partials/log-viewer` htmx endpoint (triggarr/web/routes.py:382, :1083) and rendered verbatim as `{{ entry.message }}` in triggarr/templates/partials/log_viewer.html:67/80, which auto-refreshes every 5 seconds. So the token does not just land in `docker logs` (the intended 'operator-only' channel) — it is also returned in an authenticated HTTP response body.
findings.title: Password reset token logged in cleartext and surfaced in the authenticated web UI log viewer
findings.why_it_matters: This token is a bearer credential that can be redeemed to reset the operator's password (full account takeover). The new code's own comments assert an explicit invariant — 'The token NEVER appears in any HTTP response body, header, or template context' — but that invariant is false: because the token bypasses the existing redaction allowlist, it flows into the same in-memory log buffer that feeds the dashboard's live log viewer, so any party with an authenticated session (cookie, X-Api-Key, or Basic auth — all equally privileged in AuthMiddleware) can read the token straight out of the web UI within ~30 log lines of the mint, with no need for host/docker access at all. It also conflicts with the project's own absolute rule to never log sensitive tokens.

findings.problem: The live-token no-op path (lines 1662-1676) returns immediately with no disk I/O, while the mint path additionally awaits `run_in_executor(_write_reset_token_file, ...)` (lines 1697-1700) before responding. Both paths return byte-identical response bodies, but the mint path is measurably slower due to the synchronous atomic file write + fsync, giving an unauthenticated caller a potential timing oracle for whether a reset is currently in flight.

findings.why_it_matters: Knowing whether an admin currently has a live, unredeemed reset token in flight is minor intelligence on its own (the token value itself is never exposed by this path) and would only matter alongside another way to intercept or guess the token; this is a note, not a demonstrated exploit.

agent_notes: Blast radius: the change is purely additive. It adds two new routes (GET/POST /reset/request), one module-private helper (_write_reset_token_file) and new imports (tempfile, generate_reset_token). No existing public signature changes, so none of the 16 importers of routes.py need updates.

State dependency: the handler reads app.state.last_reset_time and app.state.reset_token, which are initialized in the scheduler.py:504-507 lifespan. Test apps that build app.state manually (for example test_auth_integration.py:92, which sets only search_lock) would hit AttributeError if they POST /reset/request. test_reset.py:75 builds its own app state, so check that it sets both attributes.

Auth exposure: middleware.py:118 exempts '/reset' and '/reset/*' with an exact-or-slash predicate, so the endpoint is unauthenticated by design. The response never includes the token, which is good. Any unauthenticated client can trigger a WARNING log line containing a live token about once per 60s. That is the intended operator channel (D-02), and the H1 live-token guard prevents supersession DoS.
No auth-mode gate: the handler mints a token even when auth.method is None or needs_setup. That is harmless but noisy, and it may matter for product semantics.

Schema/migration: none. reset-token.txt is a new sidecar file in the config volume. A .tmp file can be left behind only on a crash between mkstemp and replace, the same as the existing _atomic_toml_write pattern.
Multi-process: as the SAFETY-05 note says, the in-memory token and asyncio lock assume a single uvicorn worker. With multiple workers, a token minted on one worker would be invalid on another.
Verdict: shippable as a staged step. The only concrete defect is the unguarded mkstemp (non-fatal guarantee broken). Do not release until /reset/confirm lands.

findings.problem: Global CLAUDE.md, under the absolute Security section, states: "Never log sensitive data (passwords, tokens, PII, auth headers)." This code calls `logger.warning("Password reset token minted. Read from 'docker logs' or reset-token.txt: {token}", token=token)`, deliberately interpolating the live password-reset token value into a log line. The code comments (D-02 + RESEARCH #4) frame this as an intentional 'operator-only' recovery channel and explicitly exclude the token from the app's own redacting sink, but the written rule carries no such carve-out and is marked absolute ('Precedence: the Security rules below are absolute').
findings.title: Reset token value deliberately written to logs
findings.why_it_matters: Container/application logs are frequently shipped to aggregators, included in support bundles, or retained longer and more broadly than the config volume; anyone who can read logs — not just the box operator — gets a live account-takeover token, which is exactly the class of exposure the absolute rule exists to prevent.

dir_fd = None
    renamed = False
    fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")
    try:
        os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)
findings.fix_hint: Move the mkstemp call inside the try block (or wrap it separately) so its OSError is caught by the same non-fatal handling as the rest of the write path.
findings.problem: Global CLAUDE.md states: "Add try/except around external calls (DB, HTTP, file I/O) only where this code is the intended error boundary." This function's own docstring and inline comments declare it IS that boundary for the reset-token file write ("D-17: in-memory token is the authority; file write failure is non-fatal... Do NOT re-raise"), but `fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")` executes before the `try:` block, so an OSError from mkstemp itself (e.g. missing/unwritable config dir) is not caught here and propagates uncaught to the `run_in_executor` await in `reset_request_post`, which also has no try/except around it.
findings.title: tempfile.mkstemp() call sits outside the try/except that is documented as this function's error boundary
findings.why_it_matters: If the config directory is missing or not writable on first run, this breaks the documented D-17 guarantee that a reset-token file-write failure is non-fatal: the exception surfaces in the request handler instead of being logged and swallowed, turning what should be a silent degrade (token still usable from the log) into an unhandled-exception path.

findings.current_code:
fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")
try:
    os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)
    with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:
        ...
findings.fix_hint: Wrap `fd` in `os.fdopen` (or a try/finally closing `fd`) before calling `os.fchmod`, or fchmod via the file object after fdopen so the context manager always owns the descriptor.
findings.problem: Global CLAUDE.md states: "Ensure resources are released on every path... try/finally for everything else." `os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)` runs on the raw fd returned by `tempfile.mkstemp` before `os.fdopen(fd, "w")` wraps it in a context manager. If `os.fchmod` itself raises OSError, the except branch unlinks `tmp_path` but never closes the bare integer `fd`, and the `finally` only closes `dir_fd` (never assigned in this path) — the file descriptor leaks.
findings.title: Raw fd from mkstemp not closed if os.fchmod() raises before fdopen
findings.why_it_matters: This is a rare-trigger (fchmod must fail) but real fd leak; repeated failures (e.g. a persistently misconfigured volume) would exhaust the process's file descriptor table over time.
